text:
“That is true,” I said, letting my head fall onto Marguerite’s knees; “but I love you like a madman.”

“Well, my friend, you should have loved me a little less or understood me a little better. Your letter caused me a great deal of pain. If I had been free, in the first place I would not have received the count the day before yesterday, or, having received him, I would have come to ask you for the forgiveness you were asking of me just now, and from then on I would have had no lover but you. For a moment I thought I could grant myself that happiness for six months; you did not want it; you insisted on knowing the means, and, good God, the means were easy enough to guess. In making use of them, I was making a greater sacrifice than you think. I could have said to you: I need twenty thousand francs; you were in love with me, and you would have found them, at the risk of reproaching me for them later. I preferred to owe you nothing; you did not understand that delicacy, for it is one. We women, when we still have a little heart left, give words and things a breadth and a significance unknown to other women; and so I repeat that, on Marguerite Gautier’s part, the means she found of paying her debts without asking you for the money needed to do so were a delicacy from which you ought to benefit without saying a word. If you had met me only today, you would be only too happy with what I would promise you, and you would not ask me what I did the day before yesterday. We are sometimes forced to purchase satisfaction for our soul at the expense of our body, and we suffer far more when, afterward, that satisfaction eludes us.”

I listened to Marguerite and gazed at her in admiration. When I reflected that this marvelous creature, whose feet I would once have longed to kiss, was consenting to let me count for something in her thoughts, to give me a role in her life, and that I was still not content with what she was giving me, I wondered whether man’s desire has any bounds when, having been satisfied as quickly as mine had been, it still reaches for something else.

“It is true,” she resumed; “we creatures of chance have fanciful desires and inconceivable loves. We give ourselves for one thing one day and for another the next. There are people who would ruin themselves without obtaining anything from us, and there are others who can have us for a bouquet. Our heart has its whims; that is its only diversion and its only excuse. I gave myself to you more quickly than to any man, I swear it; why? Because, seeing me cough blood, you took my hand, because you wept, because you are the only human being who was willing to pity me. I am going to tell you something foolish, but I once had a little dog that looked at me very sadly when I coughed; it is the only being I have ever loved.

“When it died, I wept more than I did at my mother’s death. It is true that she had beaten me for twelve years of her life. Well, I loved you at once as much as I loved my dog. If men knew what can be had with a tear, they would be loved more and we would be less ruinous.

“Your letter belied you; it revealed to me that you did not possess all the insights of the heart; it harmed you more in the love I had for you than anything you could have done to me. It was jealousy, it is true, but ironic and impertinent jealousy. I was already sad when I received that letter; I expected to see you at noon, to have lunch with you, to erase, by the sight of you, a persistent thought I had, one that before knowing you I accepted without difficulty.

“Besides,” Marguerite continued, “you were the only person before whom I had immediately believed I could think and speak freely. Everyone who surrounds women like me has an interest in scrutinizing their slightest words and drawing conclusions from their most insignificant actions. Naturally, we have no friends. We have selfish lovers who spend their fortunes not for us, as they say, but for their vanity.

“For those people, we must be cheerful when they are joyful, in good health when they want supper, and as skeptical as they are. We are forbidden to have a heart, on pain of being jeered at and ruining our credit.

“We no longer belong to ourselves. We are no longer beings, but things. We come first in their self-love and last in their esteem. We have female friends, but they are friends like Prudence, women who were once kept and who still have expensive tastes that their age no longer allows them to indulge. Then they become our friends, or rather our table companions. Their friendship goes as far as servitude, never as far as disinterestedness. They will never give you anything but profitable advice. It matters little to them if we have ten more lovers, provided they gain dresses or a bracelet from it, and can from time to time ride in our carriage and come to the theater in our box. They take our bouquets from the day before and borrow our cashmere shawls. They never do us a service, however small, without making us pay twice what it is worth. You saw it yourself on the evening when Prudence brought me the six thousand francs I had asked her to go and request from the duke on my behalf: she borrowed five hundred francs from me, which she will never repay, or which she will pay back in hats that will never leave their boxes.

“And so we cannot have—or rather, I could not have—but one happiness: sad as I sometimes am, ill as I always am, to find a man superior enough not to demand an account of my life from me, and to be the lover of my feelings far more than of my body. I had found that man in the duke, but the duke is old, and old age neither protects nor consoles. I had thought I could accept the life he provided for me; but what can I say? I was perishing from boredom, and if I had to be consumed, I might as well throw myself into a blaze as suffocate myself with charcoal.”
